metadata.goal: Identify movement groups among the provided trajectories based on their regions and analyze the resulting groups.
metadata.dataset_description: A 48-record comparison with four coarse start-region groups and trajectory-level movement, speed, distance, route-indirectness, time, and context fields.
metadata.reconstruction_note: Synthetic reconstructed GPS and timestamps are provided in trajectory_points.csv. All 48 distance profiles have been revised to reflect the requested regional distance scales, preserving trajectory IDs, start positions, mode shares, mean speeds and route-indirectness scores. These are not recovered WorldTrace observations or road-matched paths. See reconstruction_provenance.json.

point_metric_definitions.distance_meters: sum of consecutive-point haversine distances, R=6371008.8 m
point_metric_definitions.avg_speed_kmh: total GPS distance / elapsed timestamp duration * 3.6
point_metric_definitions.detour_score: total GPS distance / endpoint haversine distance
point_metric_definitions.mean_yaw_change_deg: mean absolute wrapped change of consecutive GPS segment bearings; horizontal heading-change proxy, not measured IMU yaw

insight_list.insight: The provided trajectories form four equally sized start-region groups: Brooklyn, Manhattan, NJ side, and Queens each contribute 12 trajectories.

y_axis.name: Number of trajectories
y_axis.description: The number of provided trajectories in each group.

plot.description: The group counts establish the regional movement groups before their trajectory summaries are compared.

insight_list.question: How many trajectories are represented in each observed geographic group?
insight_list.actionable_insight: Keep the group counts visible when interpreting regional differences; the comparison describes the provided trajectories rather than city-wide frequencies.
insight_list.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

order = ["Brooklyn", "Manhattan", "NJ side", "Queens"]
df["start_region_coarse"].value_counts().reindex(order).plot(kind="bar", color="slateblue")
plt.title("Trajectories per Geographic Group")
plt.xlabel("Start-region group")
plt.ylabel("Number of trajectories")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

insight_list.insight: The geographic groups differ in their observed distance and route-indirectness summaries: NJ side and Queens have the largest median distances; NJ side has the highest median route-indirectness score; and Brooklyn has both the lowest average distance and the most direct routes.

plot.title: Distance and Route Indirectness by Start Region

y_axis.name: Summary values
y_axis.description: Median distance, mean distance, and median route-indirectness summaries by group.

plot.description: Separate panels compare median distance, mean distance, and median route indirectness so that distance and route shape are not conflated.

insight_list.question: How do the observed geographic groups differ in trajectory distance and route indirectness?
insight_list.actionable_insight: Compare distance and route indirectness as separate regional summaries; a group can have longer trajectories without having the most indirect routes.
insight_list.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

order = ["Brooklyn", "Manhattan", "NJ side", "Queens"]
grouped = df.groupby("start_region_coarse").agg(
 median_distance_m=("distance_meters", "median"),
 mean_distance_m=("distance_meters", "mean"),
 median_route_indirectness=("detour_score", "median")
).reindex(order)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
grouped["median_distance_m"].plot(kind="bar", ax=axes[0], color="seagreen", title="Median Distance")
grouped["mean_distance_m"].plot(kind="bar", ax=axes[1], color="darkorange", title="Mean Distance")
grouped["median_route_indirectness"].plot(kind="bar", ax=axes[2], color="slateblue", title="Median Route Indirectness")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Distance (m)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Distance (m)")
axes[2].set_ylabel("Path length / endpoint distance")
for ax in axes:
 ax.set_xlabel("Start-region group")
 ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

insight_list.insight: In the Brooklyn group, most trajectories are walking trips, making it the only walking-dominant group; its average trajectory distance is also much shorter than that of the other groups.

y_axis.name: Mode share or mean distance

plot.description: The first panel shows mode shares and counts for each 12-trajectory group, including different car shares in Manhattan, NJ side and Queens; the second compares mean distance.

insight_list.question: Which geographic group is walking-dominant, and how does its average trajectory distance compare with the other groups?
insight_list.actionable_insight: Use Brooklyn as the walking-dominant, short-distance group when interpreting the regional comparison, and consider movement mode alongside distance.
insight_list.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

order = ["Brooklyn", "Manhattan", "NJ side", "Queens"]
mode_counts = df.groupby(["start_region_coarse", "travel_mode"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0).reindex(order)[["car", "walking"]]
shares = mode_counts.div(mode_counts.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
mean_distance = df.groupby("start_region_coarse")["distance_meters"].mean().reindex(order)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))
shares.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, ax=axes[0], color=["#4477aa", "#ee9944"], title="Movement Modes (12 trajectories per group)")
for j, region in enumerate(order):
    bottom = 0
    for mode in ["car", "walking"]:
        value = shares.loc[region, mode]
        axes[0].text(j, bottom + value / 2, f"{value:.1f}%\n(n={mode_counts.loc[region, mode]})", ha="center", va="center", color="white" if mode == "car" else "#222222", fontsize=10)
        bottom += value
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 100)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Share of trajectories (%)")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.27), ncol=2, frameon=False)
mean_distance.plot(kind="bar", ax=axes[1], color="#339988", title="Mean Distance")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Mean distance (m)")
for j, value in enumerate(mean_distance):
    axes[1].text(j, value + mean_distance.max() * 0.02, f"{value:,.1f}", ha="center", fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, mean_distance.max() * 1.15)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("Start-region group")
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=25)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

insights: The provided trajectories form four equally sized start-region groups: Brooklyn, Manhattan, NJ side, and Queens each contribute 12 trajectories.

The geographic groups differ in their observed distance and route-indirectness summaries: NJ side and Queens have the largest median distances; NJ side has the highest median route-indirectness score; and Brooklyn has both the lowest average distance and the most direct routes.
In the Brooklyn group, most trajectories are walking trips, making it the only walking-dominant group; its average trajectory distance is also much shorter than that of the other groups.
summary: The provided trajectories form four equally sized regional groups. NJ side and Queens have the largest median distances, NJ side has the highest median route indirectness, and Brooklyn combines the shortest average distance with the most direct routes. Brooklyn is also the only walking-dominant group, so movement mode remains part of the regional comparison.
